Under the lock, the rate-limit double-check and the live-token guard are both correct. The token is assigned inside the lock before the file write happens outside it, and the 60s limit stops a second mint from racing that write.

findings.fix_hint: move mkstemp inside the try (initialise fd/tmp_path to None and guard the cleanup on them), or catch OSError around the run_in_executor call
findings.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` runs before the `try:` block. The docstring promises that an OSError is non-fatal (D-17) and is never re-raised, but the `except OSError` handler does not cover mkstemp. Any of these makes mkstemp raise: a read-only config volume, a full disk, a missing parent directory, or EACCES on the config dir (common with Docker/NAS bind mounts under a mismatched PUID). The error then propagates out of `run_in_executor` in `reset_request_post` (line ~1698), and nothing there catches it. By that point the token has already been stored in `app.state.reset_token` and logged, so the client gets a 500 instead of the neutral confirmation. The guarantee the docstring states does not hold on this path.
findings.title: mkstemp sits outside the try, so a failed temp-file create turns a minted reset request into a 500
findings.why_it_matters: A config dir the app can't write to is a likely setup in exactly the situations where an operator needs recovery. The reset page errors out, even though the token was minted and logged.

findings.fix_hint: call os.fdopen first and fchmod via f.fileno() inside the with, or track whether fdopen succeeded and os.close(fd) otherwise
findings.problem: `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` runs before `os.fdopen(fd, "w")`. If fchmod raises OSError (for example EPERM on some network or FUSE filesystems), the except branch unlinks tmp_path but never calls `os.close(fd)`. The `finally` only closes `dir_fd`. The descriptor stays open for the life of the process. The whole acquire-to-release scope is visible in the hunk.
findings.title: Raw fd leaks when os.fchmod raises before os.fdopen takes ownership
findings.why_it_matters: Each failed attempt leaks one fd. It's rate-limited to 1/min, but the leak is unbounded over a long-running daemon.

findings.fix_hint: use a dedicated reset lock (e.g. app.state.reset_lock) for the rate-limit/token critical section
findings.problem: reset_request_post takes `app.state.search_lock`, only to serialise the rate-limit and token state. scheduler.py:131 holds that same lock for the full search cycle, which includes outbound HTTP calls to Radarr and Sonarr. During a slow or hung cycle, the reset request blocks until the cycle finishes or the watchdog steps in (scheduler.py:600-660). The work inside is purely in-memory state, so a dedicated asyncio.Lock would avoid the coupling. pending: confirm typical search-cycle duration makes this user-visible.
findings.title: Unauthenticated reset request waits on search_lock, which is held for whole search cycles
findings.why_it_matters: An operator recovering a locked-out instance can see the reset page hang for the length of a search cycle.

findings.fix_hint: unlink any existing reset-token.txt before minting, or when the write fails
findings.problem: When the current token has expired, a new one is minted. If the file write then fails, the handler only logs it, and the reset-token.txt left over from an earlier mint keeps the expired token. The operator is told to check reset-token.txt and finds a token that will be rejected. Nothing in this diff deletes the file on expiry. pending: confirm the /reset/confirm path or expiry handling doesn't delete reset-token.txt.
findings.title: An earlier run's reset-token.txt stays in place when the new write fails
findings.why_it_matters: The operator gets a token that is no longer valid and can't tell why recovery fails.

logger.warning(
    "Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}",
    token=token,
)
findings.problem: The newly minted CSPRNG reset token (generated at line 1679, full account-takeover credential for /reset/confirm) is passed directly into `logger.warning(...)` as the `{token}` placeholder. Comments at lines 1682-1688 state this is deliberate and that the token is intentionally excluded from `collect_secrets()`/the loguru redacting sink that every other secret in this codebase (session_secret, password_hash, API keys) goes through (see triggarr/logging.py's create_redacting_sink and triggarr/startup.py collect_secrets). The same value is also written in plaintext to reset-token.txt (line 1697-1700). Both source (mint) and sink (log/file write with the raw token) are directly visible in the diff.
findings.title: Password-reset token logged in cleartext, bypassing the app's own secret-redaction sink
findings.why_it_matters: This directly contradicts the project's own 'never log sensitive data' convention and the user's absolute security rule against logging tokens/passwords. Anyone who can read container stdout/logs (log aggregators, shipped logs, a shared host, support bundles, misconfigured log retention) or the config volume obtains a live token that is sufficient to reset the admin password and fully take over the application, without ever touching the HTTP layer. The code explicitly carves this token out of the existing secret-redaction allowlist, so the one hygiene mechanism the app already has for exactly this class of problem does not apply here.

findings.problem: `_write_reset_token_file` (lines 1557-1595) writes the raw token to `reset-token.txt` with correctly restrictive 0600 permissions set before rename, which is a defensible, access-controlled implementation for the intended recovery channel, not a weakening. The diff does not include any code that deletes or overwrites this file once the token expires (900s) or is consumed — a stale valid-looking token can sit in the config volume indefinitely. No consumer (a /reset/confirm handler) is present in this diff to evaluate whether cleanup happens elsewhere.
findings.title: Reset token persisted in cleartext file with no expiry-based cleanup
findings.why_it_matters: If a later consumer never clears this file, an old (expired) token value remains readable on disk by anyone with 0600-level access (same user/root, or an unencrypted backup of the volume), which is a minor but avoidable secret-at-rest exposure. This is capped as a low-confidence note because the permission handling itself is sound and the missing cleanup step may simply be implemented in a not-yet-merged confirm handler.

Dispatching the synchronous file write via asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor matches the existing convention (routes.py:612, 805, 844; scheduler.py:363, 451).

Setting fchmod on the temp fd before os.replace is stronger than the existing post-rename os.chmod pattern (config.py:257/298, routes.py:615/1202/1465/1514/1538). The codebase now has two permission-setting idioms. Worth converging on fd-level fchmod everywhere later.

The neutral confirmation message string is duplicated verbatim in both return paths of reset_request_post (live-token no-op and fresh mint). A module constant would keep them from drifting, and Phase 73 owns the final wording. That's 2 copies, below the rule of three, so it is not flagged.

findings.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` runs before the `try:`. If the config volume is read-only (EROFS), owned by another UID (EACCES) or out of inodes or space (ENOSPC), mkstemp raises OSError. The `except OSError` handler never sees it. The exception travels through `run_in_executor` into `reset_request_post`, which has no handler, so the operator gets a 500 instead of the neutral confirmation. By then the token is already minted (line ~1680) and logged, so recovery still works through docker logs. But the user sees an error page, and the docstring's promise ('Do NOT re-raise', 'file write is non-fatal') does not hold for the most likely failure, an unwritable directory. Separately, if `os.fchmod(fd, ...)` raises, the raw fd is never closed because `os.fdopen` has not wrapped it yet. The except branch unlinks tmp_path but leaks the descriptor.
findings.title: tempfile.mkstemp sits outside the try block, so an unwritable config dir returns HTTP 500 and breaks the D-17 non-fatal guarantee
findings.why_it_matters: Docker deployments often mount the config volume with mismatched UIDs or read-only. In those cases the documented recovery flow shows a 500 page, which tells the operator recovery failed even though the token is in the logs.
